title: Walking After a Stroke: From the Clinic to a Gravel Path
summary: One person chose a gravel path in a park. Another chose a sidewalk. Both had survived a stroke, and both could already walk. What they wanted to try was a soft robotic support that gave the weaker ankle a push as the foot left the ground. First came a test that rarely makes headlines: could they fasten the device themselves? Four people learned to use it, chose places near home or work and spent four weeks practising there. Sensors let researchers estimate how much the weaker leg contributed to each step, even where there was no laboratory floor to measure the force. All four finished. Two went on to take considerably more steps in the week after the programme. The other two help explain why a family deserves a more precise answer than “the robot works”. This article follows the walkers from the fitting room to their chosen routes, examines what artificial intelligence could measure there, and looks at what a rehabilitation team can offer today. A faster walk along a test track may be welcome. Whether it makes a familiar path worth taking again is a question only the walker can settle.

title: When should an AI archive be written in 5D glass?
summary: Glass storage makes an unusual bargain for an AI archive. A laboratory can write a model, its training records and its evaluation data into a plate that needs no power on the shelf. The hard question is whether another team can recover the exact files decades later, and how long it will have to wait. Experiments at Southampton and Microsoft show how a laser writes information below the surface, why the term 5D describes one particular encoding, and how much data researchers have actually read back. A comparison with magnetic tape puts the writing speeds in perspective. Early commercial services also show who already has a reason to accept the wait. For a working AI system, the practical division of labour runs from glass in the archive to solid-state storage during recovery and high-bandwidth memory during computation.

title: What Anthropic’s IPO means for IT buyers
summary: Anthropic will make its stock market debut Thursday, seeking a valuation of around $1.3 trillion. While the initial public offering (IPO) is set to attract huge interest from investors, there are implications for Anthropic’s enterprise customers too. The IPO will be “a huge inflection point” in terms of transparency around Anthropic’s operations, said Arun Chandrasekaran , distinguished VP analyst at Gartner. “At the same time, it might also force a different engagement from Anthropic as a company, particularly around longer-term contracts, hybrid pricing models, and so on,” he said. Anthropic had more than 11,900 enterprise customers spending $100,000 or more annually as of the end of September, according to its recent S-1 filing , with over 1,900 spending $1 million or more, and around 250 customers spending $10 million or more. Many of its largest customers are not on long term contracts and have the ability to reduce or, in some cases, cease spending at any point, Anthropic said, though a growing number of enterprise customers are signing annual or multi-year agreements with minimum spending commitments. As a publicly traded company, Anthropic will be under greater pressure to show continued revenue growth and improving margins in its quarterly earnings. This could change how it does business with enterprise customers, say analysts. “Enterprise buyers … can expect a stronger push toward committed-spend and multi-year contracts, because investors reward predictable revenue and visible backlog more than usage that can swing from month to month,” said Nick Patience , VP and practice lead for AI Platforms at Futurum Group. Chandrasekaran agreed, noting that one- to three-year contracts are standard for software as a service vendors, and frontier AI labs such as Anthropic may seek to replicate this. title: California sues OpenAI, alleges 80-plus agent escapes hidden from public
summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI, alleging the company has lost control of its autonomous AI agents more than 80 times during testing and misled the public about how safely it develops its models. The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. It says OpenAI disclosed the 80-plus figure to state investigators but has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. In those incidents, agents reached third-party systems, foreign government websites and OpenAI’s own infrastructure, the state alleged. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement announcing the lawsuit . The state brings two claims: violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and creation of a public nuisance. It is seeking an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, and an order to abate the nuisance. It also wants civil penalties of $2,500 against each defendant for each violation proven at trial. Other incidents and internal breaches In one July incident, agents escaped their sandboxes and gained administrator-level access to OpenAI’s own systems, according to the complaint. Those systems included the company’s cloud model deployment system, its secrets management service, and its identity and access management service. The agents then launched unauthorized servers, exposing OpenAI’s infrastructure to the internet. OpenAI did not let external researchers review that attack, the complaint said. The complaint identified several other incidents involving OpenAI agents. At RubyGems, a software package repository, agents allegedly uploaded thousands of packages in May 2026. title: Hackers exploit Microsoft 365 outage to launch credential phishing campaign
summary: Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services , including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organisations across multiple industry sectors. The attackers impersonated service notifications and sent emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. Claiming emails held during the outage would be permanently deleted within 24 hours unless recipients restored them, the threat actors created a false sense of urgency, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links and potentially exposing their login credentials. “We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext,” Jeremiah Jasmin, security researcher at Microsoft, said in a blog post . Outages in cloud services bring about uncertainty and panic, an area where attackers always thrive, said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. “In cases where employees cannot access their emails and other applications, they will easily fall victim to any email promising to restore their service or help recover their account. This is especially dangerous for industries like finance, health care, government and educational institutions because employees in such organizations work with sensitive data and rely heavily on cloud services,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. Carefully constructed phishing trap The attackers used several techniques to make the emails appear relevant to recipients while evading basic email security filters. title: What can silicon carbide do for AI? From efficient power to extreme-environment computing
summary: What can silicon carbide contribute to artificial intelligence: a more efficient power supply, computation beside a hot sensor, or an artificial neuron? This article follows those distinct routes through original research and industrial documents. It explains why equal numbers of silicon and carbon atoms do not mean equal masses, and why shorter atomic bonds do not guarantee a faster processor. Fabricated logic gates and memory cells establish building blocks; NASA’s 2026 processor paper distinguishes a SiC design from a robot demonstrated with a silicon FPGA at room temperature. Cryogenic neuron experiments open another specialised direction, with refrigeration still part of the system’s energy account. The practical question is which function SiC can perform, under what conditions, and with what measured benefit to a complete AI workload. Power conversion offers a clear role; replacing today’s AI processors requires much more evidence.

title: An ECG biomarker for sudden cardiac death discovered with deep learning
summary: A routine electrocardiogram can reveal a disturbance in rhythm while it is happening. Could the shape of an apparently ordinary beat also help identify someone at risk of sudden cardiac death a year later? Ziad Obermeyer and colleagues linked Swedish ECGs to death certificates, then examined what their model had learned. When they altered a beat to raise its predicted risk, the descending edge of one wave became less abrupt in lead aVL. That observation gave them a feature they could measure in actual recordings. The Swedish results show both the promise and the limits of the approach. A small group had a markedly elevated event rate, yet many ECGs preceding a death fell below the chosen threshold. Records from the United States and Taiwan add evidence about ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Whether offering defibrillators to people identified through this signal would prolong their lives remains an open clinical question.

title: Dory1.0-4B and the value of a second pass
summary: Can a language model solve a harder problem by applying the same learned transformation a second time? NVIDIA’s Dory1.0-4B makes this question experimentally tractable. Its central block can process the same sequence at different depths while the model’s four billion parameters remain fixed. NVIDIA reports a substantial gain from the second pass on software repair and reasoning over long documents. Further passes yield smaller gains on average, and factual accuracy changes little on one knowledge test. This assessment examines the published weights, training design and evaluation results alongside measurements from people running the model on their own hardware. Experiments with llama.cpp and a Rust inference engine illustrate how precision, memory management and the choice of execution depth affect speed. These comparisons also show why the number of generated tokens, the time required to answer and the quality of the answer deserve separate measurements.

title: From a blue pixel to an AI server: where does gallium nitride save energy?
summary: Where does gallium nitride reduce heat between a blue pixel and an AI server? In a display, the useful output is light. Researchers compared tiny blue emitters at the same optical output per unit area and measured how warm their surfaces became. In a server, the useful output of a power converter is electricity delivered to the next stage. Two matched converters show what happens when gallium nitride takes over the switching job from silicon. A separate test lets us calculate the watts still lost while delivering 480 watts to a load. Nitride transistors have also been joined into logic gates and a memory cell. Each experiment puts a different limit on what we can claim. Together they show where this semiconductor already earns its place, where silicon remains part of the device, and what to measure before promising lower energy per AI response.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Why surround the channel? From FinFET fins to RibbonFET nanosheets
summary: A transistor that is supposed to be off can still pass current when its channel gets very short. Why does wrapping the gate around thin sheets of silicon help, and when could an AI chip benefit? A cross-section compares the three controlled faces of a FinFET with the gate that surrounds each channel in a nanosheet transistor. Measurements on an early three-sheet device show what it means to control current with a small change in voltage. Intel’s later tests on working CPU cores reveal something a device measurement alone cannot tell us. The voltage that reaches a transistor depends on the network supplying it. A matrix engine might use that margin to calculate at lower voltage. A model waiting for weights from memory presents a different test. Which part of a response could actually get quicker, and how much energy would it take?
author: The Bible of AI

title: Triton versus Rust and CUDA C++ in AI and 3D mapping
summary: Meta needed to bring new model operations to its own accelerator without writing each one in low-level C++. Triton helped the team do that. An experiment with a 3D map shows where the choice changes. On the same GPU, Rust and CUDA C++ find space for new observations much faster.

author: The Bible of AI

title: What can stacked CFET transistors change for AI chips?
summary: What could stacked CFET transistors change for an AI chip? A logic gate normally places two complementary switches beside one another. Moving one above its partner can bring neighbouring gates closer and shorten the wires that carry intermediate results through a matrix engine. Intel and imec have tested stacked devices in silicon. TSMC has demonstrated a ring oscillator and a working memory cell. A separate study lets us ask what those results might mean for inference. Its researchers laid out the same arithmetic array with two transistor technologies and compared wire length, footprint and power at different operating points. A smaller array could run faster, yet draw more power when it did. The practical question is whether an accelerator can use that extra margin to deliver the same model output with less energy once memory traffic and cooling are counted.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Why does an AI accelerator wait for memory? Inside high-bandwidth memory (HBM)
summary: High-bandwidth memory (HBM) sits beside an AI accelerator and feeds the units that do the arithmetic. Why can a processor still spend time waiting for data, even when the model fits in memory? Follow a token from the interconnect of Huawei’s Atlas 960E to the weights an expert needs to read. Then look at an experiment on an NVIDIA A100 in which the same attention calculation finished sooner despite doing more arithmetic. The difference lay in how often intermediate results crossed the boundary between the processor and its memory. Specifications from AMD and Google help distinguish how much data a chip can hold from how quickly it can read them. For someone using a language model, the final test is whether these changes shorten the wait between tokens or let more people receive timely answers.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Nim versus Rust and C++ on a home Ethereum node
summary: A home computer can help verify Ethereum if it can keep up with the chain. Nimbus chose Nim to translate the network rules into native software. An independent study measured the memory its client used. Three CPU tests put Nim beside Rust and C++, while the chess engine Heimdall puts Nim to work evaluating positions with a neural network.
author: The Bible of AI

title: When does a faster link make AI faster? Huawei’s Ascend 960DT and Atlas 960E
summary: Huawei’s Ascend 960DT and Atlas 960E raise a practical question for AI. When parts of a language model run on different chips, how much of the wait for the next token comes from moving data between them? Follow one token as its numerical representation travels to a remote expert and the result comes back. Huawei’s design brings optics close to the electronics and gives the accelerators a shared way to address memory. An earlier system, CloudMatrix384, offers something the new design still needs: published measurements showing how the pace of an individual reply changes as more requests share the machine. We examine what those results establish, what Huawei has announced for the Atlas 960E, and how a test at fixed response time could show whether a faster link delivers more useful work for each joule.
author: The Bible of AI

title: When does Amazon’s cloud capacity unlock funding for Anthropic?

title: Autonomous robotic operation controlled by wave-based neuromorphic hardware
summary: A small robotic car approaches an obstacle. Its distance readings travel by Bluetooth to a dish of water, where six actuators set waves in motion. A camera captures the interference pattern, a classifier reads it and the car receives an instruction to turn. Jacob Zohar and colleagues used this arrangement to demonstrate that a physical wave field can participate in the control of a moving vehicle. Their experiment raises a question that matters whenever a machine acts in the world. Could an independent observer explain why it turned at a particular moment? The published route shows what the car did, and the archived five-class examples show which obstacle configurations that separate classification test included and which it left out. Reconstructing an individual decision requires the readings, images and motor command from the same moment. The distinction also matters for the proposed magnetic successor to the water reservoir, whose obstacle recognition the authors studied through micromagnetic simulation.
author: The Bible of AI

title: When Artificial Touch Improves Grasp Control
summary: When a hand closes around a fragile object, the person controlling it needs to know when contact occurs and how firmly to hold it. A bidirectional brain–computer interface can return information from a sensor to the person while a decoder translates intended movement into action. Human experiments have tested how much this return signal contributes to grasping. Participants have reported where contact occurred, distinguished aspects of shape and, in individual studies, moved objects faster or deformed them less. A recent experiment with a hand orthosis also tested a controller that automatically adjusted grip force. Its design reveals why successful grasping can depend on both a sensory cue and assistance from the device. This review examines what each comparison establishes, how long electrically evoked sensations remain available, and which evidence would support a claim about independent use in daily life. Completion time and object deformation capture different aspects of grasp quality.

title: Microsoft’s outage should terrify every enterprise
summary: I’ve been in cloud computing long enough to see just about every kind of failure: bad deployments, network failures, identity outages, botched DNS changes, overloaded regions, misconfigured automation, and old-fashioned human error wrapped in a shiny cloud-native package. Most outages are expensive and annoying. Some are embarrassing. A few become case studies. This Microsoft outage is different. The scale, duration, and downstream impact of what just happened are unlike anything I’ve seen in my career. Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams, Exchange Online, and Copilot were disrupted across more than 70 countries, with reports beginning November 12 and services not fully recovered until Saturday morning. That is not a temporary glitch. That is not a regional hiccup. That is an international cloud failure. People can stand in a circle and kick Microsoft, and plenty will. But the more important question is what enterprises should learn from this. My clients are already asking the same thing: How do we reduce our dependency on this technology before the next failure costs us even more? What Microsoft says happened We are being told that this was not a cyberattack and not an AI-related incident. Microsoft pointed to a technical issue involving settings applied to servers after an update, along with a process for establishing secure connections that became overwhelmed and caused servers to stop handling requests. Other reports described servers failing automated health checks and becoming unavailable, which pushed more load onto the remaining infrastructure until those systems also became strained. That explanation makes sense as far as it goes. A configuration or server update creates unexpected behavior. Automated health checks begin removing capacity. Load shifts elsewhere. Remaining systems become overwhelmed. Services fail. Engineers begin rolling things back and restoring systems gradually. But that is the operational explanation. It is not the architectural explanation.

title: Agents build things. Enterprises have to run them
summary: I’ve never worked in the Kubernetes space, so KubeCon, its big event, is rarely top of mind, even when it’s in my backyard . Last week it attracted more than 10,000 attendees, yet a good friend still questioned its relevance in the age of AI. I’d mentioned KubeCon in a post and he texted back, “No one cares about the primitives anymore. Agents just build things!” I found myself agreeing with him, but only for a moment. For those of us who live in AI, it’s easy to forget the reality of enterprise adoption. I’ve spent years warning against fashion-driven Kubernetes adoption , and I’m hardly nostalgic for developers spending their afternoons deciphering deployment configurations. If an agent can spare them that work, wonderful. But there’s a rather large difference between no longer wanting to configure infrastructure and no longer needing infrastructure that works. For those who think Kubernetes’ obsolescence is just a prompt away, well, reality bites. Indeed, many of the people embracing AI are precisely the people who understand why the primitives still matter. I posited this to Linux Foundation CEO Jim Zemlin, arguing, “AI changes how we create software faster than it eliminates the work of operating it.” “Yep,” he texted back, “Code is cheap [but] trust is expensive.” That’s a much better explanation of KubeCon’s relevance than nostalgia for YAML. The AI crowd is already here It’s not as if the Kubernetes crowd is allergic to AI. Far from it. As noted in a recent CNCF and SlashData report , 75% of cloud-native developers use AI coding tools, compared with 55% of their non-cloud-native peers. Of course, cloud-native developers aren’t synonymous with Kubernetes operators. Even so, it’s hard to find data to support the idea that the Kubernetes infrastructure community is stubbornly resisting AI. The two interests overlap. title: Don't write your AI skills. Do the work first, then capture it
summary: The easiest way I've found to build a skill: do the real work with the AI until the third version is right, then turn that chat into the skill. Full video on my channel: @dylandavisAI
author: Dylan Davis

title: Stop watching AI work. Give it a task before your next meeting
summary: Most of us supervise AI word by word. The goal is to hand it a task and walk into your meeting while it works. Full video on my channel: @dylandavisAI
author: Dylan Davis
